Petition to the hon. House of Commons assembled _
The petition of the undersigned humbly sheweth:
That a portion of the Peigan Indian reserve has been leased to the Hon. A. J. McLean, although a large majority of the Indians voted against the lease;

Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary):	I
desire to ask the Minister of National Defence if a requisition has been made to the Adjutant General for military assistance in connection with the Cape Breton situation. If so, what assistance has been asked for, and what is the number and composition of the troops actually furnished and proposed to be furnished?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou, Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: TROOPS DESPATCHED TO STRIKE AREA IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
The situation in regard to the despatch of troops is as follows: General Thacker, who is in command of the district in which the difficulty arises, in response to the requisition of the Attorney General of Nova Scotia, sent to the scene of the disturbance in the latter days of last week 260 troops of the permanent force

Miners and Steel Workers
from the city of Halifax. Further requisitions were made by the Attorney General of Nova Scotia upon General Thacker, and by virtue of the power conferred upon him in the statute which was passed last year under which he is sole judge as to the number of troops that are required, he requisitioned the Adjutant General for additional troops. I have not all the telegrams here, but those that I do happen to have I will read: At five minutes after twelve, midnight, the following message was received from General Thacker by the Adjutant General:
Mayor, Sydney Mines, requests military protection to-night Sunday. Feared mob will burn wholesale stores. Mayor of Sydney requested for military protection feared strikers will loot city to-night Sunday. Cannot give protection as no troops available. Urge that further reinforcements in view of widespread area affected at least 500 additional to troops now on their way.
At 4.20 a.m. this further telegram was received from General Thacker:
Mayor of Sydney mines requested military protection twice to-night, Sunday. Mob looting Mutual grocery stores. Mob 300 reported marching from Florence to join mob at Sydney Mines. 23.30 hours: Mayor of Sydney requested military protection. Feared that mob would loot city. Cannot give as no troops available to act State of terror rapidly developing in area. Small mob set fire to petrol stores outside Dominion No. 2. Officials extinguishing hindered by mob which was dispersed by troops. G.O.C. and G.S.O. proceeded Cape Breton by troop train leaving Truro this afternoon, Sunday. Reported rioters are in possession of one machine gun but are without ammunition, also that man left Sydney for purpose of obtaining ammunition.
The result was that in the last two days troops from St. John's, Que., Toronto, and London have been ordered to the scene. I have not got the exact figures with me but I will be very glad to give them later to my non. friend.

the act now stands the Labour Department can undertake conciliation. At the present time the troops of the federal government have gone to that area at the request of the Attorney General of the province of Nova Scotia under the statute. He was asked to come to Ottawa on Saturday, and he consented tp Mr. Murdock going down to the area, being on the ground so that we could have first-hand information as to what was going on; and he is to act as a conciliator, as a mediator, between the men and the company with the consent of both. speechtext: I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Graham) why the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act as amended respecting national emergency have not been carried out. Mr. R. V. LeSUEUR (West Lambton) moved in amendment:
That the Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved
That in the opinion of this House export of hydro electric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearly license, and no license should be issued beyond those at present outstanding except for off-peak power.
He said:	I am moving this resolution because the question involved is of grave importance to this Dominion; because I feel that it would be unwise to permit the session to close without this House recording definitely and clearly its attitude on this question of the export of power; and because I believe the resolution has merits and is both reasonable and practicable. I will endeavour to be concise in my statement of the matter.
In the first place, allow me to say that we as members of this House, no doubt have in a more or less general way a realization of the important place which hydro-electric energy to-day occupies in our national life; but I doubt whether a clear, ample, and serious appreciation of just how great a factor hydroelectric energy is in our national life to-day or how great a factor it is destined to be in our future development, can be had without a fairly detailed study of the growth and history of hydraulic power, and without a study of the uses to which hydro-electric power is put to-day. Such a knowledge and such an appreciation is possessed by men like Sir Adam Beck and Mr. J. B. Challies, men who have deveoted the greater part of their lives to the study of this question, and whose disinterested and consistent efforts towards the development of our hydro-electric power are well known. I wish to quote a few of the statements of these gentleman and their statements are entitled to much more weight as to this phase of this question than any

Export oj Power
statements I can personally make. Mr. Challies, in July, 1924, delivered an address at the World Power Conference in London on The Water-Powers of Canada. Mr. Challies was then the Director of the Dominion Water Power and Reclamation Service, and as showing the importance to us of our water-power development, I wish to make a few quotations from his address on that occasion. He said:
During approximately the last decade in Canada, while the population increased 22 per cent, the water power developed increased nearly 100 per cent, the use of water power in industry 245 per cent, and the capital invested in manufacturing industries 175 per
cent	But the water power now developed in
Canada amounts to 3,227,414 horse power and represents, including transmission and distribution, a capital investment of $688,000,000. Despite the continuous development that has taken place in the past and the 750,000 horse power of new construction now in hand, the demand constantly exceeds the supply and it is estimated that some $300,000,000 of additional capital will be needed to meet the actual power demand of the next ten years.
Again he says:
The extensive use of hydro-electrical energy is largely dependent upon and evidence of its low cost. Plate No. A-3 illustrates the source and character of the power supply for the industrial centres of the Dominion, and shows that water power not only completely dominates the situation in central Canada, where no native coal is found, but it also controls the market for industrial energy in the maritime provinces and British Columbia where excellent coal is found.
When referring to particular industries he makes some statements which I believe will enable this House to grasp in some detail just how important electrical power is to our industries. He says:
Pulp and paper manufacturing is a typical and important Canadian industry with a prosperous future, the result of two natural advantages,-abundant supply of growing pulpwood and cheap accessible motive power -in large quantities. The importance of low cost power lies in the fact that it takes practically 100 horse power to produce one ton of paper per day. It is not surprising, therefore, that motive power used in this industry is almost altogether restricted to hydraulic energy and that Canada's premier advantage and position in the pulp and paper field rests on adequate and abundant water power well distributed among extensive timbered areas.
He refers also to mining as follows:
The mining industry of Canada owes its present rapid development to water power, even coal mines use hydro-electric energy where possible. The metalliferous mines of northern Ontario now utilize in excess of IOC,000 horse power of hydro-electric energy and the development of further water power sites is rapidly proceeding in order to overtake the demand for energy. If the mines of Ontario had to depend on imported coal for their power requirements, the greatly increased operating cost would, in a great measure, have throttled [DOT] their productiveness, making the working of any but the richer deposits unprofitable and seriously reducing both the annual production and profitable life of the properties.
After stating that the total installed horsepower in Canada has grown from 975,000 to 272
3.227,414 horse-power since 1910, Mr. Challies goes on to say:
There is every reason to believe that this rate of growth will not diminish. New uses for electric current of the greatest import in industrial processes and services are being constantly discovered. Canada's strategic advantage in the location of large reserves of water-power within transmission distance of her centres of population should attract special industries to these centres in increasing numbers. Population follows industry and at once an added market is created for power for domestic and municipal uses. All the modern tendencies in the utilization of cheap power indicate that the rate of growth of hydroelectric development in Canada will increase rather than lessen.
Allow me also to refer to a statement made by Sir Adam Beck in presenting the annual report of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario for the year ending October 31, 1923. He says:
Industrial conditions throughout the province during the year have been considerably below normal, with a consequent reduction in the demand for power for industrial uses. Notwithstanding this adverse industrial condition, there has been a considerable growth in the demand for power on all systems, and on several systems the commission has reached the limit of the capacity of the existing generating plants. It is, therefore, necessary for the commission, on practically all systems, to make arrangements to secure additional power developments to meet the ever-increasing demand.
Sir, I read these quotations as being the statements of men well versed in the hydroelectric power situation of this country, and as evidencing not only the importance of hydro-electric energy in our present municipal, social and industrial life, but also the prospects for its rapid growth and its dominance of our markets for industrial energy.
Now, then, let me say a few words as to why I consider the resolution which I have moved necessary, and why I believe this House should, before the close of the session, definitely place itself on record on this question of the export of power. Some three weeks ago a file was tabled in this House, and in that file we find a letter which in part reads as follows:

Carillon Industrial Corporation Limited.

I will do so as briefly as I can, because these leases have already been discussed and I do it simply as a step in my argument. The first point which we note in this draft lease is that if it is executed and made binding it would grant to the lessee water-power privi-

Industries that build up their fabric upon hydro-electric energy depend upon these conditions; and these conditions existing, if we attempted to withdraw our hydro energy from any foreign community such action would I think constitute a proper case for diplomatic intervention on the part of any government in the interests of its nationals.

In days when the value of electrical energy was not so high as it is to-day and when the industrial life of the country was scant and meagre in certain communities, especially where nature had endowed the country with undeveloped water-power, the expense of the financing and flotation of hydro electric propositions being also as heavy as it was, it became necessary that an immediate market should be found for the energy thus developed and1 an immediate income and return should be at the command of those who were pioneers in the movement. Be that as it may, and notwithstanding that the companies which had been financed by bond flotation found it advisable to carry out a policy of exporting power on long-term contracts at a very low rate to ensure the return of an adequate revenue to the promoters and to make the sale of securities safe, that being an important factor in the industry, I still think that nearly all of the promoters of these companies, who had vision enough to go into the business, have found that it has been a great mistake. Mr. Speaker, at the time of adjournment I was talking about the electrical power shortage in Ontario, and I had been referring quite extensively to Sir Adam Beck. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I make any references to that gentleman with a great deal of confidence. He has devoted his life and broken down his health in the struggle to insure cheap and plentiful hydro-electric power to the people of his province, and I think that the protest he has made on this particular occasion is but a further evidence of his public spirit. No one can very well doubt Sir Adam Beck's testimony not only having regard to the man himself, but also to the facts. No one can be so foolish as to suggest that there is not a real shortage of power when at the present moment an appropriation of ten million dollars is being made for the purpose of generating power by steam in a province that ought to have access to these powers and the benefit of their full and complete development. Why Mr. Speaker, we have heard statements made by hon. gentle-

Export of Power
men particularly interested in the district of Carillon with respect to the necessity of work being provided for the people in the locality. I would point out to the House that last year an application was made by the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission for leave to develop this very Carillon site-not for the purpose of exportation, but for the benefit of Canadian consumers. So far that application simply stands.
In this particular case we have not only a common interest, but a declared common interest between the central provinces-Ontario and Quebec. Their protests against the exportation of this power are united, and are voiced by those best entitled to speak-by the premier of each province and by those interested in the production of electricity, the power companies on the one hand in Quebec and Sir Adam Beck on the other hand in Ontario-all taking a common Canadian stand. Their interests are indeed common. For example, both provinces are directly interested in the production of paper. Neither province can make any success in that production without cheap and plentiful power. In order to turn out one ton of paper every twenty-four hours a supply of 100 horse-power of electricity is needed; and none of us think that the development of our wood pulp resources is at an end. Yes, our interests are common. The metallurgical mine-s of Ontario require a good deal of electricity in their development. Those well posted say that the mining development of Ontario has only commenced, yet with that commencement to-day we are using 125,000 horse-power. Quebec has similar opportunities, she is expecting to rival Ontario's mining development and will require a great deal of electrical energy for the purpose. Indeed, without electrical power we might just as well abandon any thought of the successful exploitation of our northern mines. To get coal up there on the present scale of costs and freight rates would be absolutely prohibitive and would effectively retard the development of any but the very richest deposits. I repeat, both provinces are united in their protests. Those protests surely are well founded; their interests are in jeopardy. The door should be locked and bolted, and then doubly locked and bolted again to prevent the exportation of this precious Carillon water-power.
There is a great deal behind this Carillon proposition. Early in 1923 the associated industries of New England took up the question of their power resources and the possibility of getting power. A committee was appointed, expert engineers were engaged, and
the work put in hand. A very excellent report was got in 1924, a report which covers pretty fully all the waterqrowers of Quebec and the remaining water-powers of Ontario, because that investigating committee very wisely thought the only water^powers that Ontario had left were the water-powers of the St. Lawrence, and of the Ottawa and its tributaries. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have got within this report our water-powers catalogued up to a distance of some 475 miles. There is a great deal behind this application. If this
400,000	horse-power by any unfortunate action gets across the line, there will be an annual saving in New England territory of approximately $4,500,000. The prize is great, and the efforts are strong, and they are still going on; they are going on notwithstanding everything that took place in the House on this question not so very long ago. Why, it is only last week that the bonds of the old company were purchased, and so far as I can find out, were purchased at a slight premium, at 102, I think, but I am not definite on that point. But the bonds were purchased, and the pressure still goes on. Those behind the movement still think they have such arguments as yet undisclosed as will enable them to force the hand of the government.
I referred to this report. It is an interesting report. It is very interesting in that it shows us what a great asset we have in connection with our water-powers. It shows us again what a tremendously important thing electricity is, what a tremendous development there is for electricity, even in territory like the territory of the New England states, where but a very small percentage of the electricity produced is produced from water, where practically all the electricity is produced by fuel-burning plants.
There is confirmation in this report of what has been said on the question of the water-powers that are still available, those little powers here and there which in the total amount to a tremendous quantity, if you like, but which are non-existent for practical purposes. I commend this report to the very careful study of the government. If they study it, and really appreciate it, there will be no more export of electricity from Canada.
This report points out at page 99 how very small the power is which New England obtains, or can obtain, from her own water-powers, as compared with her demands, which are met by fuel-burning plants, and proceeds as follows:
The greater part of the undeveloped water power in New England must wait for the growth of local demand

for power because in most cases the cost of development would be too great to justify the added cost of transmission to different centres of demand. Even if the 'local restrictions on the taking of power from Maine were removed,-

-the high cost of development and transmission would prevent the exportation of a large proportion of this power.
That is just exactly the position of a very large number of the water-powers to which reference has been made by hon. gentlemen who were mistaken enough to justify in this House the exportation of Carillon power, powers which they referred to as powers to which Canada can look for her future supply. The New England states are not so foolish as to think that powers of such a character are of any practical and immediate use whatever.
The report, after dealing with their own local powers, proceeds to deal with the Canadian situation, and there is a map in here which I would again draw to the government's attention, map No. 17, which illustrates the Canadian situation. It shows the available water-powers. They show the available water-powers in On'ario, those in the St. Lawrence, and the Ottawa, with its tributaries. The report also is very interesting in showing just what can 'be done with power, and where power would go to. It is interesting also as showing how important electricity is, and how much is used notwithstanding the high cost of coal. Why, Mr. Speaker, the delivered cost to the consumers on (he average there is 3.4 cents per kilowatt hour.

Is there any question as to what the building up of the industries immediately to the south of Quebec is doing to that province? My hon. friend says not at all. If he had been here this afternoon he would have heard the admission from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) that eastern Ontario never had a proper supply of power. We all know that eastern Ontario has been beggared in her industrial development. Does my hon. friend rejoice in that fact? There is great danger, Mr. Speaker, that irreparable injury may be done to Canada unless in some way or another we

are protected. I look upon this resolution as something in the best interests of the government, and I am absolutely sincere when I say that. This campaign is no new thing and it has been going on, not for weeks, but for months. Indeed it is a matter of years and it is ready now. Here is the report and here is the market, and there are the bankers, the great financial house in Boston of Harris, Forbes & Co; interested as they are in maintaining the commercial interests of the industries of the Neiw England states. There is something ahead. There is $4,500,000 to be saved if this thing can be got and taken away at the expensed Canada. It is in the very best interests of the government that this resolution be adopted, and that this pressure should be removed from them. This pressure is all the more dangerous, if the Prime Minister knows nothing about it, although it goes on for a length of time. It has been going on now for a long time-these revised drafts, bearing on their faces the evidence of careful preparation. It is absolutely in the interests of the government and everybody else that the resolution should pass as it stands. It is in the interests of Canada that this question should be settled. I hope the government will take this resolution in the spirit in which it is offered. It is not intended as a want of confidence motion, but they can turn it into that if they so desire. We in Ontario as well as our friends in Quebec are deeply interested in this question. We want to see Canada left with a plentiful supply of electric power for the development of her natural resources, for the development of our paper and pulp industry and for a greater development of the yet unknown Eldorado of the north in both of these provinces, which is only possible with cheap and plentiful power. I therefore support the motion, Mr. Speaker.

I have listened attentively to
the discussion of this important subject for many hours, and I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot understand the attitude of my hon. friends to your left. I do not know what shivers have taken hold of them in the past two years. They seem to be embarrassed on account of the extra powers we may develop in this country in connection with our hydroelectric. In all the provinces of the Dominion we have power to develop, and no doubt in many provinces there will be a surplus of power that should be sold somewhere outside of our own country. if they had no market for their produce outside of Canada, what would they do with the extra quantity of wheat that they produce? and they would pay for it just the same amount as would be paid by a Canadian consumer. The 2,000 horse-power does not represent the rights of the Americans as far as the international boundary is concerned. The international boundary on each side of the river covers a distance of seventy miles. The Americans are claiming only 2,000 horsepower, whereas we are going to develop between 50,000 and 75,000 horse-power. They do not claim even one-fifth of their rights according to the agreement which I have just read. This water-power is developed on Canadian soil entirely, and according to the engineers the dam that will be built will allow the water to flow back for a distance of only fourteen miles, that is fourteen miles out of a distance of seventy miles as far as the international boundary is concerned. Our American friends are willing and ready to give us what we are entitled to. In order to make this development a success, while a certain quantity of this power will be needed to fill our requirements at home, we feel that we are going to develop more than we need at home, and for that reason we want to have the power, not under the Dominion government, but under our provincial rights, to sell outside the extra power that we shall have on hand.
Therefore, I would suggest that it would be very apropos for the House to arrive at this conclusion, that the export of hydro-electric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearly license, and that hereafter no license for export of power beyond that already granted should be issued except with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power. That means that no power should be exported out of any province by the Dominion without the consent of the province where the power is developed. Let me appeal to my hon. friends from the west. moment that our water-powers are one of the great natural resources of Canada. It does not need any very vivid stretch of the imagination to realize that some day we shall likely require for use in Canada substantially all the water-powers which we have developed and undeveloped at the present time. But being one of the great natural resources of this Dominion, those water-ipowers which are undeveloped now should be utilized either in the development of Canada or for such purposes otherwise in the sole interest of Canada itself. In other words, although I believe the water-powers undeveloped at the present time will eventually be needed for use in Canada alone, and for that reason it seems it would be an extremely unwise thing to export any (of that power whatsoever, yet at the same time it does not seem to me entirely wise or in the greatest interest of Canada immediately to shuit the door and say that we shall never at any time export any of those water^powers, because the occasion (might arise-and we do not know when it might arise; we cannot even say whether it ever will arise-when it might become vitally necessary, in the interest of this country for bargaining purposes or for other reasons, to utilize certain of these water-powers in procuring some other greater advantage for Canada. It seems to me therefore unwise for us in this House to-day to shut the door definitely and absolutely for all time and say that we shall never export water power.
My hon. friend from West York this evening has emphasized the various necessities for the water-powers of the Dominion. He has read extracts from various reports and has placed the situation before the House in a very lucid and fair manner. But I do not think that there are many of us who needed to be told all that that hon. gentleman has told us. We realize all these facts to the full. We realize on this side of the House just as much and indeed more than hon. gentlemen realize opposite the great importance of doing every thing possible to develop this Country to its very fullest extent; and I do not think that hon. gentlemen opposite can point to us and say that we do not desire to preserve for use in the development of the Dominion our water powers or any other natural resources which are in the country. The preservation and use of our natural resources has at all times to this government been a matter of the greatest concern, and I have no reason to believe that this policy will 'be' departed from in any respect so far as our water-powers are concerned. It is true that there are a number of undeveloped water powers in this country

and in this vicinity. In the Ottawa valley there is undeveloped water-power to the extent of at least 350,000 horse-power; while on the Rouge river there is power to the extent of over 20,000 horse-power, on the Nation over 20,000 horse-power, on the Lievre over 80,000, and on the Gatineau over 150,000 horse-power, all undeveloped. The casual observer might ask, what is the use in allowing all this water-power to go to waste? I do not follow that theory at all. I have no hesitation in declaring that I am not in favour of the export of water-power except in the case of some actual necessity which is shown to be of distinct benefit and advantage to this country, nor am I in favour on the other hand of absolutely closing the door forever against such export, and taking the stand that we should never under any circumstances permit the export of water-power.
If parliament closes the door cannot parliament open it again, should the contingency ever arise?

Parliament is expressing
an opinion at the present time, and there is no occasion so far as I can see for parliament to come to any other decision than that our water-powers should be used for the general advantage of the nation. I see no reason why we should at the present time irrevocably decide against the export of water-power at any time should it be deemed advisable but at the same time I say definitely that at the moment I would close the door not only against the export of water-power on a
9 p.m. one year lease, as is contemplated by this resolution, but also -against the export of off-peak power. There is no reason before the House or the country just now why we should export any power at all, whether it b'e off-peak or otherwise.
My hon. friend for Restigouche and Mada-waska (Mr. Michaud), properly placed before the House very largely the same opinion I had intended stating myself. The export of power, I take it, is governed 'by the federal laws, while the utilization of that power is governed largely if not entirely by the respective provinces. In other words, the Dominion exercises in this matter, as it does in regard to many other matters, a general supervision, while the provinces exercise a specific supervision over such matters as come particularly witihin their own purview or within their borders.

Does the hon. gentleman
suggest that the provinces have any constitutional power with respect to the export of water-power?

Export oj Power

I am not suggesting that.
I shall be glad if the hon. member will correct me; but as I understand the law, the export of water-power is not within the jurisdiction of the provinces, even if in any case that power is entirely within the province, without the consent of the Dominion. That is the law on the subject. I was proceeding to say that while the Dominion exercises a general supervision over the export of power, yet the provinces themselves control the question as to what shall be developed within their own borders-what their specific requirements may be,-whether or not the industries which require development should be assisted, and in the same way whether it is in their interest to develop water-powers, to refuse export or to export.	-
The views of my own province on this subject are well known in this House, and I adhere to those views. Without any hesitation whatever I say that so far as the province of Quebec is concerned the attitude is that water-power should not be exported; and I am in accord with the government of that province in that regard. But I do not agree with the terms of this resolution, that there should be no export of water-power except as regards off-peak power. I go further than that and say that without the consent of the province, wherein there may be any development, no water-power whatsoever should be exported. I do not think that anything could be clearer than that; I do not think that any opinion Could be more honestly expressed in this House than the attitude I have stated on my own account as to whether power should be exported or not. Exportation does not rest with the province as a matter of law, although it may be a question of expediency with the province as to whether or not a certain thing should be done in the interests of that province. A grave question must be faced in connection with many inter-provincial water-powers, and that is as to whether one particular province or another owns a certain water-power. And that urges me to express the view that it is for the provinces to act in co-operation with the government of the Dominion and vice versa with a view to deciding whether it is wise or not in any given case to export water-power. When such a question comes up for consideration, then I think is the proper time for a decision to be reached in a matter of this description.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should be sorry if anything in this debate would misrepresent the attitude of the province of New Brunswick with regard to 273i
water-power development. It is true, as my hon. friend from Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) was saying, that the province is about to embark upon a very large expenditure for this purpose. I do not think that the people of New Brunswick wish to add very largely to their capital debt merely for the purpose of getting back a bare return upon the outlay by the sale of power to a foreign country for the upbuilding of industries there rather than within the limits of the province itself. I think New Brunswick can be described as a unit in desiring the fullest and most extensive development of water-power within its limits for which a market can be found. Now, what must that market be? The development of our wood resources principally, to a minor extent the application of electricity to farm purposes, and incidentally, of course, the lighting of cities, towns and villages. The export of power from New Brunswick would mean that for every unit exported a precisely similar development would be sustained in the state of Maine in competition with the development of our own natural resources. No New Brunswicker can want that. What we do want is this development within our own territory. It is the one opportunity that we have. I feel that the people of New Brunswick will stand by me in regretting any suggestion that we are simiply going into the development of water-power for the purpose of exporting it and building up a foreign country at the expense of our own resources.
Now, I have no fear that this amendment in any way touches the situation of New Brunswick. It does not. As my hon. friend from Restigouche and Madawaska has explained, the International Joint Commission has approved of an arrangement which has been made. They declined, and I am very sorry that they declined, to enter into a discussion and ultimate decision of the question as to whether or not the state of Maine had any right to demand a portion of this power. As a matter of fact it is not really the international boundary that is in question; there are very large areas of the watershed within the state of Maine, without the utilization of which it would be impossible to develop the project at Grand Falls to its ultimate capacity. The province of New Brunswick has no right to go into the state of Maine and demand to be allowed to place dams there and pen back that water; and the state of Maine, in my judgment, has no right to say that the consideration for so doing shall be the sharing of the power. But the action
Export oj Power

of the International Joint Commission has virtually treated it as such, and I notice that an arrangement has been completed for the export of about 2,000 horse-power to the state of Maine, which has accepted this as an equivalent to what it claims as its proportion. It bases that not at all on the figures given by my hon. friend, but on the view that it would be entitled to one-sixteenth of the power produced, which it estimates at about 50,000 horse-power. An arrangement has been made that a certain concern in the state of Maine shall receive this 2,000 horse-power annually.
The International Joint Commission having approved of that arrangement, we must remember that the commission acts entirely under a treaty to which this country, as part of the empire,, is a party. It has the force and effect that all treaties have by section 132 of the British North America Act, which provides that:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof as part of the British Empire towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
Therefore the 2,000 horse-power that will go out under this arrangement from the province of New Brunswick will go out not as an export controllable by this parliament, but as a fulfilment of a decision or as approval by a body which has sovereignty in the matter, that is the International Joint Commission, based upon a treaty, which treaty must be supported by any legislation that is necessary, and that legislation must be enacted by this parliament. We are obligated by the British North America Act to do it. So if legislation to the fullest extent were to be based upon this amendment, it would not affect the arrangement that has been made with regard to New Brunswick, or any other arrangement which would be imposed as part of a bargain approved by the International Joint Commission.
Further than that I do not feel any special interest in the question, except on the general ground that what we can utilize for our own development should be utilized here and not sent out of the country to compete with us. It is no way to build up our own country. Hon. gentlemen may view the matter in any way they like, but it is morally impossible to continue the practice of export over a long series of years and then deny the people who have been getting the benefit of the exported power the right to continue it. It is all very well to say that they understand you will put an end to it. It is not the way that one decent

neighbour would act towards another decent neighbour who had done him no harm, and countries must be controlled by the same principles that would apply to citizens. Therefore before any power is exported and rights to it acquired, it is only fair I think for us to say to our neighbour, "Look here, we are going to need all this for ourselves, and we are not going to increase the quantity that you now get," That is the principle we should apply. But every man within hearing of my voice, every man who is interested in the question, knows there is something more immediate, something more insistent than that. We know that it is only by the advocacy of this principle at this time that a willing government is being rendered afraid to take a step which will be disastrous to Canada.
