I maintain that we should stop this exportation and go no further; otherwise we shall not have sufficient power to supply our own towns, cities and rural communities in Ontario.
Although the aggregate load distributed to the rural dwellers is, and must always be, but a relatively small proportion of the total energy distributed by the "hydro", its influence upon the economic life of the province of Ontario will doubtless be far-reaching and is already a factor of importance. Agriculture still ranks as the most important of our industries and in these days with farm labour scarce and expensive, anything that takes its place ^ is a great help to the farmer, for, as is universally ackowledged, upon him, in the last analysis, rest the prosperity and welfare of the community. Hitherto the rural resident has thought chiefly of electrical service in connection with lighting, but his greater need is for convenient power. The appliances that are so helpful to the city dweller, such as washing-machines, irons, fans, etc., are of even greater help to the farmer's wife; but, in addition, the farmer can make use of a large number of devices which are even more labour-saving than those used in the city, such, for example, as water-pumps, cream-separators, churns and milking-machines which can be all operated by quite small motors. Where electrical service of larger capacity can economically be installed, additional machinery, such as buzz and drag-saws, choppers, root-pulpers, ensilage-cutting boxes and threshers, for which the farmer usually employs auxiliary power, can also be operated electrically.
I should like to find out from the government what has been done with the Ontario government's application to develop and distribute power on the St. Lawrence at Morris-burg. The application of the hydro has been before the Dominion government for two years. Has it been refused? I may say that this is a very important problem for the people of Ontario, because you have only two sources of power supply left in eastern Ontario, namely, the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. As far as the eastern portion of the province is concerned there is an abundant supply of potential water-power to be obtained from the river at Morrisburg and the Long Sau'lt rapids. This is an international portion of the St. Lawrence river. The province of Ontario owns 130 per cent interest in that power, amounting to 800,000 horse-power. To sum up: Ontario gave to

Adam Beck the chief stewardship of $160,000,000 invested in hydro on behalf of 2,200,000 shares in Hydro properties. The results that Adam Beck achieved by his stewardship of Hydro are set down in the following statement.
_ 1- Every dollar of the $160,000,000 Hydro investment is earning interest and sinking fund.
2.	Hydro investment saved Ontario from a coal famine that would have bankrupted the province in war time.
3.	Hydro investment saved 2,200,000 shareholders over $75,000,000 in reduced coal, light and power bills.
4.	Hydro investment saved Ontario over $100,000,000 on coal prices, which would have gone to $30 per ton in war time but for the Hydro investment that gave Ontario the equivalent of 3,000,000 tons of United States coal per annum.
The force in the national life of Canada that most truly proved itself Liberal in the best sense and Progressive in the best sense of those two much abused words, Liberal and Progressive, is the force represented by the Hydro Conservatives in Ontario. The triumphs achieved by the Hydro Conservatives of Ontario under the leadership of Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck have cut Ontario's coal consumption in half, and cut 75 per cent off Ontario's light and power bills.
They seek to get 300,000 horse-power from this Carillon development and export it to the United States, and once the power is exported to the United States as in the case of the Ontario Power Company and the Niagara Lockport Company it is gone forever. Power once gone is gone for all time to come; once exported it is always exported1. That is a principle that is true in hydro development here, and all the world over. In the case of the Niagara Lockport Company the power exported is used by the American municipalities for commercial and domestic lighting of all kinds. Look at the trouble you have got into over the Chicago diversion of water. Water has been taken illegally as not intended by the people of this country. Most of the courts and the press and the people say it has been "stolen." They have taken that water at the rate of 10,000 second-feet, equivalent in horse-power to 35 million dollars a year. That is the equivalent of the electrical energy from the water which has been illegally taken. If you have had international trouble over the water that has been wrongfully taken at Chicago, what kind of trouble will you have if the power derived from these waters is exported forever? Certain legal questions have arisen which no doubt will go

Export of Power
to the Privy Council, because all that Canada is interested in is the surface water for navigation jjurposes, For example, at Port Col-borne, the federal government takes all it needs for the purpose of navigation and the water required for the Welland canal. The surplus waters, subject to the rights of navigation belong to the province of Ontario. Half of the Niagara river subject to navigation belongs to the province. The province of Ontario owns the bed of the river halfway out, and the banks and rapids of the Niagara river. That is its physical property and the interest it has in those waters. I think the Privy Council, if a specific case went to it, would so decide, but the question of federal export tax and license is very doubtful, Mr. Speaker.
An international question has arisen, not only from the international standpoint I have referred to, but also from the legal side, as to what international rights the United States and Canada have in those boundary waters, and secondly what rights the provinces have in these navigable waters.	Some of the
license rights claimed, I contended about a month ago, especially in the Niagara district, are illegal and it is very doubtful if the Dominion has the power, although the Minister of Justice said that his department had given its opinion that the export tax was intra vires.
I will support the amendment because in my opinion the day for the further export of power and any extension of it is gone. I agree with the second clause of the resolution that no license should be issued beyond those which have been issued, but I do not agree with the proviso which says "except for off-peak power."
There is no such thing as cheap power exported as off-peak load power. Any electrical engineer will tell you that. In the case of power exported to Lewiston and Lockport, which is exported and distributed by the Niagara-Lockport Company you cannot turn off the power during peak hours. You cannot shut off the power exported in the industries on the streets of Lockport at peak hours. They require to have that power available for twenty-four hours a day for 365 days in the year. They cannot go behind that contract for 60,000 horse-power which has twenty-five years yet to run at S12.35 per horsepower. The time has come now to hearken to the warning and adopt a proper policy in this connection. It is said they may cut off yur coal supplies, but there are two sides to that question. That matter was discussed in this House a short time ago. Great Britain
seeks at present a market for her surplus coal. There is an overproduction there and [DOT] they have an accumulation of 10 million tons of coal which should be brought to Canada, and we should obtain all our coal supplies from countries under the British flag. We need not pay attention when they say they would cut off our coal supply, because there are two sides to it. It is deplorable to go to Lewiston, continue on up the river and see the connected chain of factories from Lewiston all the way to Niagara Falls and to Buffalo. Why are those factories there? That is a concrete example of the futility of the policy of exporting power. All those factories are linked up there and why? Because of the generous, magnanimous and foolish policy of the government in exporting power from Ontario to the Niagara and Lockport district. Starting on the Canadian side from the village of Queenston what have we? Queenston is situated right opposite Lewiston, but you can go to Queenston right up to the falls and on to Fort Erie and hardly see an industry. There is hardly an industry along that river front except at the falls, Chippewa and Bridgebury, all the way up to Fort Erie. Why? The industries are mostly on the other side because of the export policy. Further on, up to the city of Buffalo what have we got, as a result of the policy of exporting hard grain and power. We find twenty-eight elevators have been built in Buffalo and are there to-day, and in the Toronto Globe we will see a reference to one of the largest companies in Canada, the Maple Leaf Milling Company, conducted by Mr. D. A. Campbell, with head offices iin the Dominion Bank building. The Globe says:
It is interesting to note that overtures have been made to induce Maple Leaf to establish a mill at Buffalo.	_
And why? Because of this foolish policy in Canada of exporting hard grain, power and raw material and because of the foolish policy in many other lines in regard to grain and other matters. I believe there is a great deal of truth in the words of the late President Roosevelt, where a similar situation arose in his own country when he was in power. In regard to the waste of water-power in the United States he predicted that the day was not far distant when the United States would run out of coal, natural resources, particularly petroleum and gas. He said:
The people of our country are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than has been ever seen, as it affects very closely their domestic and industrial iife. Our next generation will witness a shortage of those natural resources, petroleum and gas. The price
Export oj Power

of coal will be such that hydraulic power turned into electrical energy will, owing to its cost, become the prevailing factor for transport, for manufacturers, for lighting and heating our towns. Our hydraulic power alone, entirely and judiciously employed, would be adequate for the present needs of transport, industries, municipalities and private individuals. The major portion of these powers is not developed and remains the national property. It would be madness to part, without conditions, with one of our greatest resources. If we become guilty of this crime, our children will be bound to pay an annual royalty on a capitalization fixed at the highest price that the trade will stand for. They will see themselves struggling with powerful sweaters entrenched behind the doctrine of discharged rights strengthened by all means of protection that money can buy and the cunning of corporations defended by legal men. These ogres of finance will have succeeded long before then tc monopolize those resources- so as to be able to dictate to the people the management of their affairs and their way of existence. Public opinion will be their least worry.
In conclusion, I appeal to the government of this country to-night to enable the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, having pointed out the shortage of power, to go on with this Morrisburg development. This shortage was pointed out the other day in a report made by the chairman of that commission, Sir Adam Beck. He is sick and we do not know how much longer he will be with the people of Ontario. Possibly he may not be very much longer with us. He has had to face at times in the past twenty years the opposition of both-federal and provincial governments. His health has broken down in the effort to preserve this magnificent heritage of cheap light and power founded by the Conservative party, because this was brought about by the Conservative party in the province of Ontario. It was a protectionist development in the way of preserving their natural resources for the benefit of the people of Ontario. So I appeal to the government of Canada to-day to give the right answer to the government of Ontario in order to enable them to go on with the Morrisburg development. The application has been in for two years. It will enable the commission to supply electrical energy not only for the cities and the towns and the public utilities, but in addition for the farms of the province.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the arguments presented by hon. gentlemen opposite in support of the amendment which has been moved, they seemed to fall in the main under three heads: First, an argument in support of the conservation of our natural resources; second, an argument against international embarrassment through the export of power which it may be difficult and impossible

to withdraw later on, and, third, the undesirability of stimulating through the use of power generated in Canada, industries in the States which come into competition with our industries. These three headings include, in the main, the arguments that have jbeen adduced in support of the amendment that has been proposed. With respect to the motive underlying all three contentions, I believe the House as a whole will find itself in general sympathy. Whether or not the amendment as drafted is necessary in order to have the broad principles underlying these very important considerations recognized is, I think, open to question.
In the first place, with respect to the conservation of our natural resources, if an amendment were needed for that purpose, it would I believe, be speedily given support. The question, however, is not at the moment one of the conservation of our natural resources. The electrical energy available at the present time in the central area of Canada is estimated at something between eight and twelve million horse-power, of which but 1,200,000 odd horse-power has been developed, with a capacity development of, perhaps, 3,000.000 horse-power. Electrical energy in the matter of export is not of the same character as some other natural resources, minerals, for example. Minerals, once extracted and exported, are gone. Electrical energy	is	of such a nature	that whatwe transmit	at	the moment	will	make nodifference so	far	as the future	supply is concerned. Rivers continue to flow on, and if the opportunity is lost while it presents itself, it is lost forever, to the loss of all concerned. The argument therefore, as regards the conservation of our resources beyond the point of declaring that at no time should Canada export power that she needs or may need within	a	limited time,	has	no great
application.
I am sure every hon. member would wish, with respect to the export of power to see that und'er no condition was power exported which we would likely need in the immediate future, or which we would be unable to recover before the time at which the actual need might arise. With any policy that has that end in view, the government is wholeheartedly in accord. That aim however, is met completely by the first clause in the amendment:
That in the opinion of this House export of hydroelectric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearly license.
Speaking in this House some nights ago, I intimated, as respects the present adminis-

Export oj Power
traticn, that such was the basis on which we had proceeded in the past, that it was the basis on which we were proceeding at the present time; and that it is the basis on which we intend to proceed with respect to the export of electrical energy. We intend to grant licenses for export only for a year at a time, and where electrical energy is being exported under license for that period of time, all parties must understand that one of the purposes of the reservation is that it may be distinctly understood that this country may, at any moment, without giving cause for any right of action or ill-feeling on the part of the country to which energy may be exported, . have the right to make use cf its own electrical energy as required.
As to the second point, the danger of international embarrassment once power is exported on any scale, and attempt at withdrawal is made where industries as a consequence have been built up in an adjoining country, if I recollect aright the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) stressed that point strongly when speaking in the House not very long ago, and in so doing made a special reference to myself as likely to be in sympathy with him in that regard.
I am in entire sympathy with that point of view. I do not think it is the part of furthering good relations with our neighbours to tike any course likely to occasion serious embarrassment at a critical juncture, and I believe, if electrical energy were to be exported in great quantities for a period of time without every precaution being taken in the leases made, that kind of embarrassment mi^ht arise. It wculd be most unfortunate if, in this country, we did not foresee that possible danger and take every step that a government in its wisdom should take in avoiding possible embarrassment of that character. These international frontier problems are problems which, particularly in this country with its frontier of 4,000 miles, we cannot safeguard too carefully. The reason, however, which should cause us to be careful in the matter of preventing international embarrassment in the future ought to make us equally careful in not imposing a handicap to international negotiations in the present. We in this country have to rely, to some extent at least, upon our neighbours for certain importations. We have witnessed in Canada during the winter season times when we have been grateful to the United States that she has not seen fit to shut off the supply of coal coming into our country, when she has adopted the broad and neighbourly policy of saying that she would do for Canadian industry and for the Canadian people in the matter of coal supply practically what she was doing for her own industry and her own people. That is an attitude which I submit we should not forget in any line of policy we lay down and which may be directed particularly against our great neighbour to the south. What is true in the matter of the importation of coal is true also in regard to the importation of oil. It may also be true at any time with respect to some other commodity cr commodities which we find it necessary to obtain from that country.
In addition to this, we may by going the length of the. proposed amendment, be imposing a handicap on some of ou>r own provinces in the development of their resources. Mention has been made in the course of the debate to-day of an application that was made to the United (States to permit the exportation of power to Canada at a site near Waddington in which there is a small water development on the American, side and which some of our industries wished to take advantage of, as it would have been to their interest to have the use of power generated at that point. It is conceivable that at another point in Ontario power development might take place with advantage to a local industry on the other side, where an exchange could be made with our neighbours to balance our importation from them. (Such a reciprocal arrangement would be cut off completely if we adopted any such course as is now suggested, and far from its being to the advantage olf either country it would be a distinct loss to both.
The amendment declares that no license should be issued beyond those at present outstanding, except for off-peak power. This simply means that the hands of this and all other administrations would be completely tied in the matter of international negotiations; and I submit that it is not in the interests of Canada to have her hands tied in any particular in international negotiations with the United States. We should be as free as possible in our negotiations with the United States on trade and other matters, and should possess all latitude and powers calculated to be of service in such negotiations. We may not have occasion to use them, but to the extent to which we tie our own hands we help to render impotent the power of our own government when negotiating on any relevant question. I submit that to go the length of denying the administration that power of freedom in negotiation which should be reserved to it .is simply to work an injury to the country and to render no good service in return.
Export oj Power

In regard to 'the third point which has been raised, namely, that of building up American industries at the expense of our own, the argument sounds very plausible, but we must not forget that it is also applicable 'in its force from the other side of the line as well as from our own. We obtain large quantities of coal in this country from the United States for utilization in our industries and for the purpose of running our railways. And our railways and industries are competing with the railways and industries of the United States. Would this House regard as a neighbourly act an expression of opinion from the United States congress at any time that thereafter no further exportation of a commodity which was essential to us in connection with our industries should be permitted on any consideration? I contend that parliaments exist in part to help to maintain international good will, and that the broad interests of the nation rather than any special interests <or any party consideration ought to be the controlling principle in matters of this kind. As I have already said, while we cam apipreciate the force of an argument which would seek to conserve for our own needs, and in a manner that would avoid embarrassment, whatever is essential in the way of electrical power in the country, we should take care in presenting our point of view not to express it in such terms as would place in the hands of our enemy a weapon which could be used against us, and take out of our hand the power which we need for purposes of negotiation. For that reason I wish the mover of the resolu-
10 p.m. tion (Mr. LeSueur) could see his way to amend it. I would not ask him to withdraw it entirely, but I think he might amend it in accordance with a suggestion put forward in one or tiwo speeches this evening. The amendment as it stands reads:
That in the opinion of this House the export of hydro-electric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearly license, and no licenses should be issued beyond those at present [DOT] outstanding except for off-peak power.
I would suggest that the hon. member amend his resolution by deleting the words "and no licenses should be issued", and so on, and substituting therefor the words:
-and that hereafter no license for the export of power beyond that already granted should be issued except with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power.
I believe that if that provision were substituted it would give all the security that is needed. In the first place, it is I think an advantage both to the provinces and to the Dominion that each case involving the export of power should, as it arises, be examined on

its merits. There may be a situation in Ontario and Quebec which may be of considerable concern in some directions at a particular moment. But it does not follow that arguments applicable to it apply with equal force with respect, for example, to a situation in the prairies provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. It is conceivable that in those provinces the moment may come when some export of power may be desired in order to enable the development of power within the provinces themselves.
We have a surplus of power in Manitoba now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That being so, no doubt the province of Manitoba may wish to have the right at any time to export that power, and I think it would be unfair for this government or for the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec to say that Manitoba should not have that right. So doing, on the part of the federal government, might not as respects the export of power be an interference with provincial rights in the general acceptation of that term, but it certainly would be an interference with provincial interests in that matter of the development of their resources; and I submit that the federal government, should always seek to consider the wishes and the needs as well as the rights of the different provinces that go to make up confederation, and should not take a step, by means of a resolution such as this, which might cause embarrassment to even a single province and possibly considerable embarrassment to several. In a word, if this parliament declares that there should be no export of power except by yearly license, it thereby serves notice on its neighbour-because it is only to the United States that any export can take place-that at any time, as the needs of this country demand, that power export may be terminated, without occasioning a grievance or without having established any vested rights of the other side meanwhile. If beyond this it couples with that declaration the provision that all future licenses shall be granted only by concurrence of the province from which the power is to be exported, there should be every reason to feel that we have gone as far as we should in seeking to safeguard our resources. To go further would be possibly to work an injury in the opposite direction.
Now, I do not know whether my hon. friend will accept this suggestion, but if he does not I should find it difficult to appreciate this motion being moved on going into supply for any reason other than in some way to

Export oj Power
express a want of confidence in the government. I have stated frankly the policy of the administration. It is embodied in what I have just suggested as an amendment to the motion before the House, and in order that it may be perfectly clear to the House I shall read what I should like my hon. friend to move as expressive of the policy by which the government is prepared to stand:
That the export of hydro-electric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearfy license, and that hereafter no licenses for export of power beyond that already granted should be issued except with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power.
If the last part, which is what I suggest, is acceptable to my hon. friend, the government will certainly accept the first part of his resolution.

Is it the Prime Minister's intention in the suggested amendment that if the power is developed in a particular province, the virtual authority of export should be vested in that province should the province desire to export any part of the power?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, the power to export is vested in the Dominion, and the Dominion will not exercise its power without the concurrence of the province concerned.
I know, but my point is, will the Dominion grant a license to export if the province asks for it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily. I think if there is to be concurrence on the part of one there should also be concurrence on the part of the other.

What principle would
the government adopt? Because the resolution would be silent on that question entirely if amended in the manner the Prime Minister suggests. What principle would the government adopt in determining to grant a license if the province desired to export?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I have said already, I do not think this is a matter on which it is possible to generalize. I think each case would have to be examined and dealt with on its merits. The hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) quoted a case. He alleges that by by treaty rights the province of New Brunswick can export a certain amount of power regardless of what might be said by the federal authority. There are those who hold that that is not a true interpretation, that as a matter of legal obligation the province is obliged to come to the federal government to get the right to export. I do not think where there is doubt

on such a question we should adopt a motion of the kind proposed. As I understand the hon. member for St. John and Albert, he is prepared to have that export of power granted in virtue of the treaty obligation. But if it be a fact that in law that right does not so exist, or if it is open to controversy, we may have in the interval a long legal controversy arising out of the decision by this House on the question of policy. Where there is a legal doubt of the kind, if the course we are proposing is sufficient to secure the country in its main objective, I submit it is better for us to follow that course than take a step which may occasion serious embarrassment to the provinces. As an analogous case, take other boundary waters between the United States and Canada. Along the boundary in any particular province it may be that a municipality may wish to develop its waterpower, but that it can only do so by building dams within its own territory. Inasmuch, however, as the water is international, the consent of the country to the south may have to be obtained before that step can be taken. Now, in the case of New Brunswick first cited, the consent of the United States was given to the course there adopted, on the understanding that the United States would be entitled to a certain quantity of the power generated after the installation was completed. That same condition might arise in many of our border municipalities, yet if we adopted this resolution and followed it those municipalities might be prevented from developing water-power which would be of the greatest service to them, simply because it lay beyond the jurisdiction of parliament to grant the necessary license for export under an arrangement which would permit of that power being developed. Therefore the more one considers it the more one feels, I think, that there is every reason why if in a matter of great national importance such as this we are conserving our resources and safeguarding our industries and the future, we should be most careful about taking a step which might create embarrassment in international negotiations.

Take the case of a waterpower which may be located in one province but vitally affects the rights of another province, for instance, the Winnipeg river-I am not citing that specifically, but merely as a general illustration-one province might be willing to consent to the export, but the other province vitally affected by that export, might be opposed, and yet would have no voice in
Export of Power

the decision by reason of the amendment suggested by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In what I
suggested I used the expression "with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power."

Take for instance, Ontario and Manitoba, the development of the power is in Ontario, the use of the power is in Manitoba; that is, the main body of citizens affected by any export that might occur would be those in the latter province, yet the whole development is in Ontario, and therefore under the proposed amendment Manitoba would be helpless.
The development is in Manitoba.

The development is in
part at least in Ontario. I am not limiting myself to this particular case. There might be a case where the development would be wholly within one province, but its export would vitally affect the industrial welfare of the neighbouring province. The Prime Minister, I think, appreciates my point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think what
my horn, friend says shows the wisdom of the very course I am suggesting. What my hon. friend wishes the government to do is to be considerate of the interests of the provinces. He wants us not to sacrifice the interests of one province to those of another that might possibly be affected by any export of power. I would say that such would be the point of view from which the government would wish to proceed. We would wish to consider the interests of all the provinces concerned. I do not think it would be wise in stating a general policy at the moment to define it too much, but I would point out to my hon. friend that the amendment which is before the House would absolutely prevent any bind of consideration of tlhe interests of either province in the case he cites, and if there is any merit to be urged for what he has put forward, he should be the first to see the wisdom of following what is here suggested rather than adopting the more restrictive policy which would deny the Dominion any power of discretion in such a case.
I should perhaps add in order to make my position clear, that I assume the House understands that where there is an amendment on going into supply, an amendment to the amendment cannot be moved. Had it been possible to do so, I would have made a motion in that form. I have asked my hon. friend if it is possible for him to accept my

suggestion and submit a modified amendment, instead of his own motion as drafted; if he cannot see his way to do that, I have simply to remind the House that the government ban take no course other than to regard the motion directed against us as under the circumstances, a vote of want of confidence. I have tried to avoid the necessity of a division by making to my hon. friend what I believe to be a very reasonable suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
Prime Minister if the amendment he now proposes could not be so altered as to require the concurrence of the federal government and the province or provinces affected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what I am suggesting.

Not I think so far as the
concurrence of the federal government is concerned. Is that implied in the resolution as proposed to be amended?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am saying
the federal government will not agree to give in future licenses for export except with the concurrence of the provinces. The power to give export licenses resides in the federal government, but I am agreeing that it shall not be exercised except with the concurrence of the province concerned.
So long as that is clear, it is all right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is clear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
We have often debated
subjects in this House before rather crowded numbers that were of infinitely less consequence than what is presented this afternoon, and in years after when much that is good will have been forgotten, the course parliament takes on this question will be remembered as a landmark either to our credit or to our discredit.
The resolution is clear in its terms, to my mind is unobjectionable from every standpoint, but great efforts have been made to find in some remote, imaginary contingency an occasion when the principle that we ask to be adhered to might possibly have to be modified.
Why is it that we should in the first place direct policy against the export of power? I intend to give in very simple words the reason as it appeals to my own mind. I cannot see how the reason will appeal to any of those who follow the doctrines of the freetrader. I cannot see how it will appeal to those who still have faith in maxims that are

Export oj Power
recited in this House times without number; but I believe the reason will appeal to practical men.
Oh, oh.

Yes, I mean every word. I think the policy of so directing trade currents as to keep at home the raw resources of a nation for the use of that nation itself is one approved by experience, and now all but universally in practice. Different methods are adopted. The protective method is only one, but it is the chief the world over.

Thie right hon. gentleman cannot conceive of some cases where the development of the natural resources of a province must of necessity entail the export of power if there is not in that province sufficient market for its development?

I would answer the
question were it appropriate, but inasmuch as it has nothing to do with the argument I am on, I will postpone reference to it until perhaps it will have some relation to what I am saying.
The protective method is one, and it is the most universal. It is perhaps the most effective of all. There are cases to which it cannot apply. The case before us is one where it will not apply. Others would be where a nation had certain resources far too great for immediate development to the finished state, having regard to the then population of that nation. Such cases include our own supply of asbestos and of nickle. These must be provided for some other way, but the case before us is that of power.
Power is the rawest of all resources. Power is much more rudimentary, much more an instrument of further development and production than is any other raw resource whatsoever. Power bears the same relation to the ordinary raw resources of a country that those raw resources bear to the finished products of the country. It is the instrument by which the mineral is delved from the ground; it is the instrument by which the coal is heaved to the surface. It is the most fundamental and rudimentary of all things looking to the expansion of a nation; so that the arguments, which apply in favour of directing trade currents and trade policy so as to keep raw resources for development by the people of a country apply with double force to the case of power. But if they are no good with relation to the development of our raw resources, they are equally worthless with relation to power. If they have no application to the other resources of a country, they cannot be contorted into an argument for the
preservation of power, and those who still adhere to the theory that you must follow the natural trade current, that what a man or a country owns or wants he should sell in the dearest and buy in the cheapest market, those who adhere to these things cannot on any account find any ground to stand on if they wish to preserve to a nation the power that is resident within it. But there are few of those.
I think we all agree in this House that it would be nothing but suicidal for Canada to allow the export of these irreplaceable, limited, vitally precious resources from this country! We have done so in the past. Every nation in its early years of development is compelled to permit to some extent-and now I am at the point raised by my hon. friend from Lot-biniere (Mr. Vien)-the export of its raw product. We have been compelled to in our earlier years. W e have done too much of it. But as a country develops and gets stronger, it is able to take care of these more and more, and directs its trade policy to do so. We' permitted the export of power for years. We did not permit the export of a very great quantity relative to what we possessed. But
200,000	horse-power is a large amount, and that now is under license. There is this to be said for our conduct: Not only was it in line with what younger countries are very often compelled to do, but at the time the policy grew up, the Value of this great property was1 not fully understood. The value of coal in early years was not fully understood. It has taken a longer time still to have us realize the tremendous resources that we have in our water-powers. Of far greater value will it be m the long years to come than any other single thing in the way of a material product that we possess. As electricity has advanced, as the knowledge of that science has developed, we come more and more to realize the value of what we have, and consequently we get now to the position where we do not look upon these things as we did in the earlier days.
Now why is it that we say we have reached the stage when we should export no more? Well, I state it in this way: We have reached the stage where .already we feel the pinch in certain parts of our country. In large portions we do not, but in the industrial portions of our country we have got to the point where if we permit further export we are going to find ourselves within a comparatively few years bereft of these things essential to our growth. It is said we have some forty million in this country of potential horse-power. Well, I presume we have just in the same way as we have millions of acres in Greenland, millions of acres up in northern Ontario and the North-
Export oj Power

west Territories, but in so far as the available horse-power is concerned, we have not nearly the half of that figure; and in so far as that is concerned which is within transmission range of industrial Canada, we have not more than one-third of it; and in the province of Ontario, within transmission range of industrial Ontario, we have not now more than will be overtaken and be in use within a space of not more than fifteen years, and probably not more than ten or twelve years.	t
In this I quote not only the opinion of engineers as 'I have them before me in the Engineering Journal, but the considered opinion of Sir Adam, Beck who has been closer to the problem than any other man. The situation in Quebec is somewhat different. At the estimated rate of increased consumption they will pr-oibaibly have absorbed alii they possess withnn the space of twenty to twenty-five years. Now, it may appear to some the better course to say: Let us get rid of^ what is going to waste in the meantime, and, in the words of the Prime Minister, do it only by a yearly license, do it with the distinct understanding that we can take it back whenever we like, and then all will !be well. To that we on this side of the House are definitely opposed, and we are opposed because of the lessons oif experience, and because of the reasoning that applies to our relations at the present time. Power differs from all things else. If we export power to another country that other country .gets into the position where it cannot supply what we now supply, where it can obtain it from no other .source. Power is not something that is in the world market, that another country can substitute for if a first country withdraws. Power is something which once exported becomes the foundation of a great vested right and the withdrawal of it-however closely, however narrowly and carefully it may have been provided for-becomes a practical impossibility. We found ourselves in, the position that when we needed the power badly we could not withdraw it and we found1, as well, that although we applied the system of yearly licenses the company undertook to give contracts extending over a period of time and we were bound not only by the rates secured by the industry erected bult were also bound, in a measure, by the contract although that contract had no warrant to be entered into. And if we pursue the same course in the future that we have pursued in the past, and go on 'giving these yearly licenses, we will find ourselves in a very short time in relation to that power just where we do now in relation to the poweT licenses in the past. We will find industries

gathered round us, we will find municipalities dependent upon it, we will find ourselves powerless to withdraw into our own country the resources we have once let go from our midst. I do not think there are any associated with the power industry who have any other opinion. I do not think the Prime Minister has any other opinion. I do not think any member of the government would stand and say that if we give yearly licenses now and new uses are found for new power development in Canada no matter how we may surround thie export license with safe,guards and guarantees, just as soon as those uses become established and those industries and those municipalities there become dependent upon them, we cannot withdraw it. We may as well face the facts. So, I say we should make a pronouncement against further export.
The reasons urged against it are rather ingenious. I had thought this resolution embodied what appeared to be the all but universal ' opinion of the people of Canada. If ever the people of Canada came together on any single question, a study of the newspapers of the last month would indicate they had come together on this. Throughout the length and breadth of this country there appears to be little difference of view. It all arose because of certain reports which emanated from Ottawa, respecting the Carillon power, of proposed development and of proposed export. The history of that project I do not need to review. I think the House may consider, in view of the statement of the government to-day that whatever might have been, their flirtations with this project, they have now been compelled to give it up, and there is not going to be any export of Carillon power. Because in respect of Carillon power the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are the provinces interested, and as every one knows those provinces as at present governed will not consent to any export at all. So the need of a detailed review of the history of Carillon project has gone. Whatever other results these debates have had, they have had this result-that they put back into limbo the possibility of a tragedy in connection with Carillon power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Might I remind my right hon. friend that what I said to-night was just what I said the first time this subject came up; it has been our point of view all the time.

Well, I do not think it is precisely the same. I do not say that because I intend to enter into any argument as to the difference. I know the Prime Minister

Ex-port of Power
said, as about the last word in the debate, after all along efforts had been made to get an assurance of policy, that the government intended to continue the system of yearly license. That, however, is not sufficient. In the course of that debate-it was on the same subject as this-I asked and asked repeatedly, and I directed my words to the Minister of Railways, that an assurance be given parliament that there would be no license issued in future save on a yearly basis, and no license issued at all for further export if the power was to be used for any new development industrial or municipal over there. One would have thought that assurance would have been easily given if the government had no project in contemplation in relation to Carillon. But I could not get the assurance. I tried one day and I tried the next day, but the government sat silent. So I do not think this House could take from any statement of the government on that occasion that they were opposed to a further export of power. Certainly the country did not so assume and in this connection the country was right.
Now I am coming to some of the reasons urged against the resolution as it stands. It is said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) that he is opposed to the export of power. He would go even further than the resolution. He would not make any considerable exception of off-peak power. Well, we are prepared to grant the exception, we are prepared to make the elimination. As far as that goes we will go the whole length and prohibit the exportation of off-peak power. But we did not want to have a resolution to which any reasonable objection could be raised, and there is never going to be any serious thing happen from the exportation of off-peak power. No industry in the world is ever going to invest money in a contract on the faith of off-peak power; if the demand is sufficient at home no man would ever invest money or acquire a vested right position in a contract for the importation of off-peak power.
Would my right hon. friend do me the favour of admitting that I said no power should be exported without the consent of the province in which the power lies?

I am coming to that;
that is another point. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George would go the length of preventing exportation.

Would my right hon. friend be kind enough to couple what I said then with what I formerly said? Both statements 274
should be taken together; I think that is only fair.

The hon. member's argument against the resolution first of all was this, and it was because of that argument he finally made the addition that he would allow exports only with the concurrence of the province. He said that we might have a contingency where it might pay us to make the sacrifice.
Certainly.
He said that some contingency might occur later on but his imagination did not carry him to the extent of trying to picture it to the House.
May I say that-

The hon. member finds
it easier to interrupt than he does to make an argument on his feet. Though the principle is sound there might be occasion for exception. For myself I do not know what the contingency would be. I can imagine of course in the event of war, where terms of peace were being settled, it might be easy to give up something in order to get something else; but dear me these are not laws of the Medes and Persians which we are enacting. We are only declaring a principle. The fact of the matter is that indeed the government can act without a statute at all and without coming to parliament.

The right hon. member
is enunciating the precise principle which I declared. If there is a necessity that we should export power for the advantage of Canada, then and then only would I consent to the export of power, with the consent of the provinces.
If I was enunciating the same principle as the hon. member, he should have been satisfied, but I was not enunciating the same principle.

My right hon. friend is
enunciating no principle at all except politics.

A contingency which
might arise could be taken care of at the time. Parliament can act as it will. The government would have to come to parliament on every occasion in order to take action. Can anybody imagine any case where the government would want to act in the export of power, if this resolution passes, where it would be embarrassed by coming back to parliament to settle the terms of the arrangement with another country and ask for ratification? All these matters with other countries are ratified now by parliament, but

Export oj Power

as the law stands to-day, the Export Act is such that the government might enter into a contract of any kind whatever as to the export of power and not be under the necessity of coming back to parliament. All we ask is that a principle be embodied that parliament declare its will, and if any emergency occurs in the future, that few of us could ever imagine-I do not know what it would be- the government could come back and state the case to parliament, and parliament could act if it desired on the recommendation' of the government.
The right hon. gentleman does not conceive that that provision would be a serious embarrassment for the government?

Not at all. It would
be a help to the government. The government would be far better in negotiating with another country to have to say to that country, "We must go to parliament to get this done," and anyway is it not right that parliament lay down a general policy? If the government sees something great can be gained from that policy, it is not prevented from going to parliament and saying "Here is the policy: we ask you to accept that and make a sacrifice in order to accept it;" so that this excuse for voting against the resolution is no excuse at all. It does not amount to anything. The hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George is mumbling in his seat. He surely is not asleep. Why can he not act in parliament like other hon. members, and when he wants to make a speech get up and make it, and not sit in his seat groaning and mumbling?

My hon. friend would
not suggest that I should act as he does in parliament. I should be very sorry to do that.
I do not think the hon. member ever will.
No, indeed.

Another hon. member
says that if this resolution passes New Brunswick is going to be in a fix, that that province cannot allow 2,000 horse-power to be exported in relation to a development there now impending. I think the argument advanced by the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) clears that contention away completely. Certainly anything we have agreed to in the past is covered by licenses outstanding. Anything agreed to by treaty we are going to perform. We agreed in the treaty with the United States that in

relation to international waters the jurisdiction should rest with the International Joint Commission, and that commission says that in the disposition of the power of the St. John river at a certain point, owing to certain flowage rights which must obtain in the state of Maine, it is only right that 2,000 horsepower should go there. We granted that right and agreed to it years ago, and it is not covered by the resolution. This is only finding straws in the road; they are not obstacles. It is the principle of the resolution to which we have asked adherence.

If the power company
developed on the Canadian side, would it not be incumbent on that company to come to the Dominion government to get a license to export it?

It may be technically
incumbent upon it but the Dominion government has already agreed to give the license.
No.

Yes, it has agreed by treaty to give it. Does the minister say that any discretion rests with this government as to the issue of that license; that the United States of America is in the position still that it is dependent on the discretion of the government of Canada? Absolutely it is not. The issue of the license is a mere matter of course, and would not be prevented or postponed by this resolution for an hour.
It might be.
No.
It will raise a serious question as to the issue of the bonds.
No.
Yes.

I should like the minister to try it. The passing of the resolution does not affect anything. The country has already agreed to it. It is only trying to find something in the way, and the government has industriously dug up little things. It is said, "Let us agree upon this, that we as a government will say,.'We will not issue any licenses except yearly licenses' ". So far so good; or that parliament may be said to be at one'-at least in so far as two groups in the House are concerned, and the other group has been silent up to this time. I do not want to assume to speak for those for whom I have no right to speak. But as to the rest, we cannot agree. We will not give yearly licenses for additional

Export oj Power
export except for off-peak power. To that we cannot agree, but we will agree that we will not issue licenses for any further export of power unless the province in which the development occurs agrees. I do not like the principle of that as well as I like the principle of this resplution. I do not like to see parliament surrendering its jurisdiction but this distinctly does so. I prefer parliament exercising its own right. I do not like parliament saying, "we have certain responsibilities, but we have not the courage to live up to them." We will not act even within the ambit of our own authority, unless we first get the say-so of the provinces affected by our action. I think we should declare a policy of ourselves on a great matter within our own jurisdiction, but I do not want to be too ambitious in our demands. What the Prime Minister says certainly will not cover the case. There are many powers in this country in which more than one province is interested, and the province interested most is one where the power is not developed, where the province in which the power is developed may have little population and no industrial life, but it may be situated near industrial life in another province, and that other province is the more affected of the two. There are certainly powers in the Winnipeg river in which two provinces are interested. I believe Manitoba-correcting the hon. member behind me-has more actual power sites in the Winnipeg river, more power potentialities within its boundary than Ontario, but Ontario surely is not to be told that it has no interest whatever in powers developed in Manitoba, nor the province of Manitoba to be told that it has no interest in the power developed in Ontario. Similar cases, I am told, even more striking in their relationship to this proposition, exist as between Alberta and British Columbia, and I do not doubt that cases would be found still between Alberta and Saskatchewan. That is why the Dominion has jurisdiction. I do not know that there will be cases where more than two provinces would be affected. Perhaps there would not be.
Though I do not like the principle, in order to show that we are not moving this merely for the sake of a party vote, if the Prime Minister will change his amendment and say that no license will be issued except with the approval of the provinces affected by the development, then I for one would be willing to recommend to my hon. friend that he accept the amendment suggested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite
prepared to do that. It is in accord with the spirit of what I have said.
274i	-

That will be satisfactory as far as this side is concerned. Before I sit down, I want to say a word in relation to this question which is continually raised, that if we pursue this course, we are not acting in a neighbourly way to the United States; that we may bring upon our heads retaliation, and that they have not acted towards us in this spirit in the past. I have no sympathy whatever with those words, and I want to say so with the utmost frankness. In the first place, it sounds strange in my ears that properties which are ours, in which no other country can claim an interest at all, are properties the disposition of which must be governed, not by our interest alone, but by the interest in some degree of another land. Are we not to be permitted in this Dominion, in relation to assets which are ours entirely, to pass such laws as best suit the interests of Canada-
Irrespective of reprisals?

-irrespective wholly of reprisals, for fear another country would not like the step we took, thinking it is not in their interest? Will the hon. member tell me of any country that ever acted in that way towards us?
Because, my right 'hon. friend knows it; we never acted in that way towards them.

I know of no other
country that ever acted in that way towards us. I want to make clear what I say. I do not say that in all water-powers in which we are interested, the United States have no interest. Wherever they have an interest, I would recognize it to the full and I would treat with them in a neighbourly and friendly way, but as respects our own I would dispose of our own water-powers wholly in the interest of Canada. When I say that, I want to ask my hon. friend: Does he think the United States has ever disposed of any resource of that country save with an eye to its own interests? Does, he think coal has been sold to the people of the Dominion of Canada just in order to keep us warm?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Does my right hon. friend not know that during a period of great fuel shortage in this country and in the country to the south, when the United States were being urged by some of their own industries to conserve all the coal for themselves, they took the position that they wou'd treat the people of Canada in the same way as they would their own people?
Export oj Power

Yes, that is true, but
they did it in their own interest. They knew this country could have got coal elsewhere and that the markets which they have been supplying would have been filled and would have been lost to them. I am not saying this in criticism of their spirit. Their spirit is perfectly right, but their action was dictated by a regard, not for our country, but for their own interests, and that is what dictates the course of any country.
The right hon. gentleman's argument is that there is no such thing as generosity. That is the inference.

That is his
criterion.
My criterion is this, that the greatest generosity a country can perform to the world is to look after itself.
That is selfishness.

Certainly, and if we
have reached the stage when we are not able to look after ourselves, we had better haul the flag down and no longer claim to be a country acting on its own initiative. The United States does not need our generosity. If it does, I do not know when it got into that position. The people of the United States are able to take care of themselves. They do not ask for our generosity. We are exporting to-day 200,000 horse-power. If we say that we do not intend to export any more, say so frankly and act upon our statement, have the United States any complaint? I do not know what just complaint they would have. I suppose if they acted in a corresponding way, they would say: Well, we will not export any more coal than we are exporting now. I for one would not weep very much if they took that view. I would feel that that was not doing any good to the United States, and it was certainly not doing any harm to us. Certainly let them restrict their export of coal to the coal they are exporting now. Would the hon. gentleman hang his head in fear? It would be the best thing that ever happened to us. The hon. member shakes his head.

Does my right hon. friend
contend that if shipments of coal from the United States to Canada ceased to-morrow, that would not play havoc with many industries?

I did not say that. I
said if they restricted the export to the export that is going on now.
The right hon. member has not the courage of his own convictions because if he were logical, he would stop the export altogether.

I have not the stopping
of it. They have the stopping of it.
I know that.
Then what does the hon. member mean?
Supposing they do stop the shipment of coal to Canada, that would work havoc with our industries.

As soon as the United States feel it is in the interest of the United States to stop the shipment of coal to Canada, they will stop it. It is not in the interests of the United States to-day and they know it is not. I do not think they have ever acted in the spirit of injuring another country to the injury of themselves. That is not the spirit of neighbours. But in disposing of their own ressources to their own advantage, they are behaving only as a nation is bound to do, and they have never pretended to be in favour of any other principle. The United States, if they felt it was in the interest of that country to impose an embargo on the export of coal, would not wait twenty-four hours before the embargo was imposed on the export of coal. * The same thing is true of oil. This country would not be helpless in its development. I know there would be very considerable disturbance; I know it would injure us for a time; but I know also it would very seriously injure the United States and I do not fear it. There are, however, other places where we can get coal and other places where we can get oil. This country could rise to the event. This country would be injured less than the country which acted only to hurt another even at the expense of hurting itself. All these ghosts are ghosts and ghosts alone. The United States is not going to prevent the export of coal because it pays the United States to sell coal. It is not going to prevent the export of oil because it pays the United States to sell oil. The United States to-day in more than one state would not let a single horse-power pass out of its borders. They say: Oh well, we might need a little bit of power at Watertown; we might be ready to give you a little bit somewhere else.
Waddington.

It will not matter much, because we shall not get the power.

Export of Power
We were offered it.

We were offered it, but on terms we would not accept. Does anybody imagine we are going to suffer because the United States will not sell us a little waterpower? We shall get along all right. This is a resource where we have an advantage and which we must have looking to the future development of our country. What we must do is to assert our advantages fearlessly, and we shall not wither one iota in the esteem of the United States. They will think all the more of us and they will be just as good neighbours as they ever were. No country is going to act in a spirit of generosity to us because we raise a sort of white flag and say: It will be in our interest to do this, but we will not do it for fear we shall hurt you. Let Canada get out of that way of thinking, and the sooner we get out of it, the better. We have been in it altogether to long. Consequently, in so far as this argument is concerned. I give it no strength, no weight at all. The only principle to follow is to act as to our property in our best interest. Do not injure ourselves in order to injure another. Act with regard to it only with a view to helping our own people to the utmost of our ability.
I have stated this in order that the House may know how I look upon these matters. I have not stated it because it will have any effect on a division, as I apprehend there will be no division. I accept the amendment in order that we may be united and that the whole world may know how we are travelling in relation to this great question. But I would prefer that governmental responsibility should not be shirked, and I would have preferred that it be declared once and for all that we are against further exportation; but I accept it inasmuch as I believe this amendment in its practical result will reach the same end as the amendment that was moved before, because I do not believe that our provinces will agree to the export at all. That being my opinion, I accept the amendment as now agreed to by the Prime Minister himself.
Mr. Speaker-

Before the hon. member
addresses the House, I must point out that the amendment cannot be moved by the Prime Minister. The amendment as now amended shou'd be accepted by the mover, and in order that this may be done it is necessary that the leave of the House be obtained, inasmuch as it is not usual for the mover of an amendment to amend his motion except by unanimous consent.

If the hon. member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) were allowed to proceed now, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member who moved the amendment in the first instance (Mr. LeSueur) would have the revised motion ready for the House at the conclusion of the hon. gentleman's speech.
Mr. ANDREW MoMASTER (Brome): I would not delay the House were it not that something that should be said in the debate has not so far been said. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) gave expression to an opinion that is perfectly true; he said that his words would not be acceptable to those who believe in the principles of free trade. I can agree most heartily with him in that regard. But the right hon. gentleman also said that they would be agreed to by practical men. Now, who are the practical men? Before the Great war came as a scourge to humanity the practical men had said that armaments would ensure peace, that one tariff against another would increase the prosperity of the nations, and that it was a wise and practical thing for the great imperialist nations of Europe to stake out claims for themselves in Africa and Asia. These were the arguments used by practical men, and the present condition of the world is due to the principles which the practical men carried into effect; it is due to the fact that these practical men would not listen to the idealists, whom they dismissed as stupid, foolish and unwise.
It was Gladstone who said that the longer he lived the more he appreciated the value of the principle of liberty; and the longer I live and have a seat in this House the more I disapprove of the principle of restriction. When I listen to a man of real native ability, such as the leader of the opposition, fulminating in favour of restriction, as he has done for half or three quarters of an hour to-night, I am led to believe that his real idea of national prosperity would envisage himself mournfully sitting on a desert island surrounded by a sea so full of reefs that no ship could possibly inundate that country with waves of foreign goods, and with embargoes against 11 p.m. the export of raw materials, and with an immigration department whose chief abject was to keep people out of the land. That it seems to me would be a condition which in his view would bring about great prosperity in this country. Now, I have a few words to say regarding his policy of keeping at home the raw products of a
Export oj Power

nation. These products of the nation should be exported when there is a profit in exporting them, and those who own these products will have a better understanding of what it is profitable to export than could any government that you might conceive of. This idea, that governments should direct trade channels and trade currents, is one great fallacy that has done as much harm to the progress of humanity as almost any fallacy which has afflicted mankind. Suicide for Canada, the right hon. gentleman says. I say this to him, in all sincerity, that the surest way for the Dominion of Canada to commit suicide is to surround itself with policies of restriction either on goods coming in or on goods or power going out.
Addressing myself more nearly to what the right hon. gentleman said, I want to say just a word or two. He said that in eastern Canada the province of Quebec had perhaps one-third of forty million, or about thirteen million, horse-power, and he added that within twenty years that power would be all used up, because the lines of transmission could not go further than would bring power that could be all used in twenty years. May I tell him that at the present time the city of Montreal does not use up the water-power which is generated within a radius of thirty miles. There is the great power at Lachine and there is the power at Chambly, and I am told that these great powers are not in operation to-day, the water running to waste. The development is there but the water is not being used. One argument is that if we once allow power to be exported we shall not be able to stop that export hereafter. That is a mistake. The United States is not going to be dependent on our power. The 'amount of power from Canada that could be used by the United States is very small in comparison with all the horse-power generated in that country either by water development or by steam converted into electricity. There is a tremendous amount of power generated in tihe United States, and the amount that we shall supply at any time in the future will not be so very considerable as to force it to be taken into too great consideration. There is no difficulty in that direction and it is a mistake to harp upon that string. It seems to me that if there is any danger in our dealings with the United States it will be to follow a policy of dog in the manger, because that might excite retaliation. - Reference is made to the Fordney tariff. What was responsible for the Fordney tariff? It was excited by the embargo on newsprint and by our foolidh rejection of the reciprocity arrangement. The

leader of the opposition has preached in this House a doctrine which I think is a somewhat mistaken one; he says that all the nations of the world are ruled and should be ruled by stark national selfishness. They should not think of the other fellow at all. What an extraordinary statement from a man Who a few years ago said that Canada was prepared to bankrupt itself for the empire!

Would it not have been in our selfish interest to do that rather than to have been conquered?
Mr. MeMASTER: If you put it on the ground of merely selfish interest, that is another argument. But I did not so understand the right hon. gentleman's words.
Read what I said and you will see that that is one of the grounds, and a strong one.	.
It was a ground that was not urged when my right hon. friend made patriotic statements.
Because I was misrepresented for political purposes.
The first time I had the pleasure of meeting the right hon. gentleman at Morrisburg in the fall of 1915 I know that sudh a sentiment was utterly absent from anything that he said on that occasion.

Your memory is weak.
Mr.	McMASTER:	If these are the
ghosts which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have raised, in connection with the possibility of retaliation from the United States, then I think the right hon. gentleman's own words may be compared to evil angels. On t'he whole, there is not much in the argument of my learned friend, and as the House is anxious that the question shall come to a vote I will not delay it longer.

It is moved by Mr. LeSueur, seconded by Mr. Hanson:
That in the opinion of this House the export of hydro-electric power from Canada should be permitted only on yearly license, and that hereafter no license for export of power beyond that already granted should be issued except with the concurrence of the province or provinces in which it is proposed to develop such power and of any other provinces adjacent to such development and interested therein.
Amendment agreed to on division.
The amendment has been agreed to. Therefore I do not now leave the chair unless another motion is made to that effect.
