Hon. CHARLES MARCIL (Bonaventure). Mr. Speaker, I want to crave the indulgence of the House for a few moments to refer to the interest that prevails in the province of Quebec at the present time with respect to the circulation through the newspapers of news items to the effect that a question which I had the honour to submit to the House during the course of last session had finally been settled. I refer to the inclusion in the Canadian National Railway system of the two Gaspesian railways, the Quebec Oriental and the Atlantic, Quebec and Western. These news items circulated from the capital have evoked considerable interest among the people whom I have the honour to represent, but I regret to say that as yet the question has not been solved in this satisfactory way. We hope, however, that before long a solution will be found. I am glad to be able to state that since the matter was last discussed in the House considerable headway has been effected. The Board of Railway Commissioners has visited the Gaspesian peninsula for the purpose of holding an investigation into the matter, and I had the honour in the month of October last of accompanying Mr. Justice McKeown and Mr. Commissioner Lawrence and their staff during the course of that investigation. The commissioners stopped at every station, listened to the representations of the people interested, and gave them encouragement to think that a solution might be brought about under the Railway Act. A few days after the opening of the present session the Prime Minister and three of his colleagues, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Health (Mr. Beland), were kind enough to grant an interview with you Mr. Speaker, with the Premier of Quebec, represented by Hon. Mr. Perrault, His Lordship Bi.-hop Ross of Gaspe and the leading people of that part of the country. The argument made by His Lordship Bishop Ross for the taking over of these railways by the government was that Sir Henry Thornton had come to a decision, based solely upon revenues and expenditures, without taking into account the general considerations which presumably would influence the government. Sir Henry Thornton had in effect made a proposal to the proprietors to take over their railways on certain conditions, which the latter did not think proper to accept. Therefore the deputation asked the Prime Minister and his colleagues if they could not find a solution for this long-standing problem. When these railways were completed in 1911 it was understood that the Laurier administration contemplated taking them over and merging them with the Intercolonial. An effort was made during tlie Borden regime to have this given effect to. When the late Mr. Cochrane introduced hi? measure for the inclusion of two hundred miles of branch lines with the Intercolonial railway, practically every line in New Brunswick was taken over, and one or two in Quebec, but these two lines were left to one side. During the war no progress was made in the matter, but when the new administration came into office in 1921 the people of the Gaspe peninsula felt that another effort should be made to secure for themselves some share of the benefits to which they were entitled. It must not be forgotten, Mr. Speaker, that the Gaspe peninsula is the oldest settlement in the Dominion; within a few years 'four centuries will have elapsed since Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspe. The people of the peninsula have contributed their share to the upbuilding of Canada, including the construction of the railway systems of this country, and they feel that they are entitled to that fair consideration which up to the present has not been extended to them. I am glad to know that through the breaking down of the discussion between Sir Henry Thornton and the proprietors of these two railways, another attempt is being made to try to bring the parties together through the good offices uf Mr. Justice McKeown, who has been asked to express an opinion, as a result of the investigation he made of the lines, on what would be a fair and reasonable amount to be paid. The government takes the position that owing to the financial condition of the country it is out of the question for the Canadian National Railway system to buy the two railways, but that if Sir Henry Thornton was prepared to lease them on terms acceptable to the proprietors and the railway commission, probably the government would raise no Objection.
I mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to take this opportunity on behalf of my constituents of thanking the premier of Quebec and his colleagues for their active interest in the matter; His Eminence Cardinal Begin for the assistance he has given us; His Lordship Bishop Ross for speaking a good word for the peninsula, and the members of the legislature of Quebec, and others representing both sides of politics, and in fact representing the entire population of the peninsula, for the efforts they have made to help bring about a satisfactory settlement of this question.	It is a wonder
to-day to people visiting the Gaspe peninsula that these two isolated railways have been able to continue in operation so
Export of Power

long, and that it has not been possible long ago to merge them with the Canadian National Railway system. These two railways with the limited resources at their disposal have given a much improved service during the last two years, and the railway commission has made a very favourable report on their operating efficiency. But by the mere fact of being isolated, these two railways are unable to give those through rates to the inhabitants that would be possible if they formed part of the Canadian National Railways. They have to contend against water competition during six months of the year, and under the arrangement made at the time the railway subsidies were voted in 1911, they have carried the mails for the past fourteen years every day year in and year out through the long winter months for a distance of 130 miles along the dreary Gaspe coast without receiving one dollar from the government of Canada for the service. Notwithstanding this, the service has been kept up as best it could, but it has never answered the requirements of these two counties, and our industries have left us one after the other. The province of Quebec Lumber Association went over to Dalhousie, and the mills in Bonaventure have crossed over to Bathurst. An effort is now being made by Bishop Ross and the clergy of the province of Quebec to open up new agricultural areas in the Gaspe peninsula for the purpose of keeping the people at home. Our young Canadians there are now migrating to the cities, and to the United States. We want them to remain on the homesteads, and be agriculturists as their fathers were before them. This Gaspe peninsula will never be peopled by other than those who inhabit that area or their descendants, for immigrants from Europe would never consider taking up land in the Gaspe peninsula. They would rather go into the more settled part of Canada or to western Canada. So we consider that eveiy family leaving this Gaspe peninsula is a loss to Canada, and while we are spending money abroad for the purpose of bringing immigrants info this country, for want of proper industries, for want of proper facilities, for want of proper communication with the main markets of this country we are allowing these people to go away, and they will never return. The population of this county the first ten years I had the honour of representing it, at the time we had all these industries in Bonaventure, increased by some five thousand, but in the last decade, after these industries had left the county, our population dwindled, and the natural increase was only eight hundred. Now the time has 
come to bring about a solution of this difficulty. These companies are not anxious to carry on any longer. They are merely complying with the letter of the law, and nothing more.
Sir Henry Thornton has expressed his great optimism for the future of the Gaspe peninsula. He has visited the district himself. He knows the value of its timber limits of 10,000 square miles; he knows the value of its fisheries, he knows the value of its mineral, and he is-willing, if an 'agreement can be brought about with these companies to take over these roads and operate them as part and parcel of the Canadian National system, as they were intended to be operated from their very inception, and as was announced here in 1884 in this House when at the request of Sir Hector Langevin and Sir Charles Tupper monies were voted for the building of a branch line of the Intercolonial from Matapedia to Gaspe, and as Sir Wilfrid Laurier said- in 1911, that to make these railways -pay they should be linked up with the Intercolonial. This has not been done, but the people of Gaspe have faith in the present administration; they have faith in the Minister of Railways; they have faith in the broadmindedness and patriotism of this House and government, and I hope that in speaking as I do, Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken in vain, but that the Canadian National will see that it is in its interest to take over these 200 miles of railway.
We are not asking for the construction of new railways, 'as we are obliged to vote new branch lines for the west; we are merely asking that 200 miles of constructed railway to which the Dominion of Canada and the province of Quebec have contributed in land and money subsidies to the extent of four million dollars be so utilized as to give those people fair and untrammelled access at reasonable rates to the central markets of the country. Sir Henry Thornton has declared that if he took over these railroads to-morrow he would have to cut down the railway rates 25 per cent, which is an admission that the people of Bonaventure and Gaspe have been paying rates on their products for many years past 25 per cent above what is paid on the main line of the Canadian National railway.
I shall say no more, bu't for all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I hope that -when this report is received from Mr. Justice McKeown, if an agreement can be brought about between Sir Henry Thornton and these two companies, the government of Canada will seize the opportunity for the purpose of bringing about a solution of this Long Standing trouble.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of water storage dams on Ottawa river and tributaries, surveys in connection therewith and settlement of land damages, $35,000.
This is an old-standing expenditure. Is it a necessary one each year; is it for renewals?

It is an old expenditure. It is required for the maintenance and operation and dams and sluiceways at points on the Ottawa river and its tributaries. The object is to store the spring floods and augment the low water flows, thus equalizing the run-off of the Ottawa valley throughout the year. This also necessitates the purchase of lands damaged by maintaining reservoir surfaces at high stage during the summer and autumn. For the maintenance and operation of the Timiskaming dam, $7,000 is required:; for the maintenance of Quinze dam, $9,000; for reinforced concrete slab and cut-off wall and rockfill at Timiskaming dam, $13,000; to pay land damages and other claims in connection with the Ottawa river storage, $6,000, making a total of $35,000.

I never could understand
why the government of Canada should spend so much money for the assistance of the lumbermen on the Ottawa river.

It is not for the
lumbermen necessarily.

I have understood that all this expenditure for sluiceways and dams on the Ottawa river was for the express purpose of helping to drive the logs on the river. Is there any other river in the whole Dominion where an expenditure of a similar character is made for a similar purpose? On the river St. John, and on the St. Croix, which is an international river, and upon all the other rivers that I know of the lumbermen have to provide these facilities for themselves.

My hon. friend
is under a misconception. As a matter of
fact, this item is largely for the purpose of maintaining the Timiskaming and Quinze dams. It is rather in the interests of navigation than to assist the lumbermen in their log driving.
I would suggest then, that it is in the interest of the power companies.
And navigation.

The power companies on
the Ottawa river are very wealthy companies. Just recently the Ottawa and Hull company was re-financing bonds to the extent of millions of dollars, from which the proprietors of the old company receive very handsome sums of money. My objection to the whole scheme is that this is not a matter of Dominion concern. Navigation on the lower stretch of the Ottawa river cannot be assisted to any great extent by expenditures of this character.
I think it will be found, and I know something of the history of this matter from a former Minister of Public Works in a former government, that the original expenditure was in the interest of the lumbering business. Now it is said to be in the interest of the power company, and I object to the expenditure on that ground.

Is this the National Art Gallery?

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister very briefly, and I must not delay the committee unduly, a complaint that has reached me against the Board of Governors, or whatever they are called, that there is discrimination against artists at outside points, and I am speaking now more particularly of some of the artists in British Columbia, with, I think, almost an
Supply-Public Works

international reputation. My hon.. friend will recall the names without my making any particular distinction. Some that have won great distinction because of their works of art have been unable to get their paintings included in the National Art Gallery. The point I wish to draw to the minister's attention is this: I quite approve of the general principle of very careful choice in works of art, and I know that requires men of experience, knowledge and technique; but I think the National Gallery should, as far as possible, and without doing violence to this principle, have a representation of all sections of the Dominion. A work of art that might portray, for instance, a Pacific coast scene might be different from some eastern scene, but still it would be a contribution to the art gallery. The same thing might be said of an Indian picture from some distant part of the country. While in itself it anight not be quite equal to a picture from the brush of an eastern artist, nevertheless it portrays as the artist sees it the life of that community, crude though it may be, and such pictures should be preserved in the National Gallery. I merely want to suggest to the minister that care should be taken that the administration of the National Art Gallery should be impartial, and that the chief object of portraying the life and scenery of the Dominion should be adhered to as much possible.

Haileybury-to pay to the municipal authorities the amount of fire insurance on armoury for the erection of a community hall.

This vote requires some
explanation. I think I remember something about it a year ago. What is the present status of this vote and what is the necessity of it? It seems to me it is intended to make a gift to the community as a result of a fire.

At the time of the fire in Haileybury the government had an armoury building which they had rented to the municipality to be used for recreation purposes. The citizens had insured the building to an amount of $33,500. When the building was destroyed, the insurance fell due and was paid into the consoldiated revenue fund. Naturally, the people of Haileybury were desirous that the government should reconstruct an armoury or a building of that type that would be again useful for their purposes. We took the view that probably what would be more serviceable would be a post office and customs building. We carried the vote, I think, for two years on the understanding that that would be what would be done. The citizens of Haileybury, however, objected very strenuously to that; the matter was considered very carefully, and finally it was agreed that this money which resulted from the insurance obtained on the building, would be placed at their disposal in order that they might erect a community hall or building that would be suitable for their purposes. The government will not have an armoury there, but we shall have an arrangement with the community whereby the local military units will have accommodation in that hall.

Who paid the insurance
premium?

Who will have title to
the new community hall?
I think they would like the title, but I do not know whether they will get it.

I suppose the minister knows that in Ontario there is provincial legislation covering this field. It would be rather a dangerous departure fior this government to undertake the construction of community 'halls, and I dio not see that any good ground has been shown for the vote.

I happened to be in (the Department of National Defence when the transaction took pface. The town of Haileybury paid the insurance premiums, insuring the building; and when the money came in I accepted the cheque but was Obliged to hand it over to the Receiver General. I doubt whether there is any similar situation anywhere in Ontario. Haileybury is simply asking that the insurance money be used to construct a building which they want. The Dominion does not insure buildings as a general rule; it does so only in exceptional cases. In Ithis case the town paid the premiums itself and it handed over ithe insurance money, $33,500, rather reluctantly, although there was nothing for it to do but that. At that time I thought that we should be in a position to erect a post office building or something oif that kind, but apparently that :is mot what they want; they want a hall which they can use for the same purposes as they used the drill hall before. Mr. Chairman, it
does seem to me a most anomalous situation. I think it is an admirab'e thing to erect a community hall-personally I am glad! it is to be that instead of an armoury-but I cannot see why Haileybury should have a community hall any more than five hundred
other places in this country should have similar accommodation. The reasons which the minister has advanced are by no means convincing. They seem to be based simply on some indefinite claim that Haileybury has to this $33,000. Apparently the only basis for the claim is that they paid the insurance which, as we have been told, was paid apparently as rent. That was over and done with when the building was burned down. It would seem to me that naturally the $33,000 insurance would revert to the Dominion government and should remain in the treasury until such time as it is needed in some particular place. I cannot see any special claim that Haileybury has upon this money simply because there was a temporary arrangement with regard to the former building.

Surely the hon. gentleman does not understand the situation here. Fire destroyed the town and everybody came to its aid-provincial and Dominion authorities, the Red Cross and other associations, and the public. It was decided that the least the government could do would be to replace the building burned down and leave the town in its former position. The Minister of Public Works is not going that far. He is merely contributing $33,500 to the erection of a building which, if he undertook to replace the old building, would cost the people of Canada twice as much. We are really saving $40,000 by handing back to Haileybury the insurance which was kept up by the municipality. I think it is most reasonable that in order to encourage the people to rebuild in Haileybury we should at least set them an example.

Mr. Chairman,

I understand that the term
of the present Governor General is drawing to a close. This might be a good time for us to abolish Government House altogether. I notice that in Alberta they have abolished the Government House, and I think perhaps it is a good thing to do. However, if it is to be maintained, I hope that we shall have the office filled with a Canadian-born Governor General, not that I have any reflection to cast on any Governor General, but-if the office is to be maintained, I hope it will be filled by a Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
think we ought to let that statement pass unchallenged. I would like to know how it would be possible to select a Canadian Governor General under the present party system of this country, and who would be satisfied with the selection? The "ins" might be satisfied, but the "outs" certainly would not. The main reason however, for continuing this office, is that the Governor General is the one great connecting link between the people of Canada and the Crown of Great Britain, and I hope the present method of selection will never be changed or the office abolished.
? I feel there ought to be a word said about that myself. The present occupant of the office of Governor General is one-	.

One of the real
men.

I call him a real man,
not' standing on a pedestal at all, but down among the people. He has visited every part of the Dominion of Canada, and both he and Lady Byng have become of us and with us in a way that is commendable to all the people on this side of the ocean, and on the other side. It is disappointing to a great many of us that they could not see their way clear to remain for another term. His Excellency starts to-morrow on a trip up to the northern

Supply-Public Works
hinterland of Canada, and when he goes back to London, he will prove to be one of the greatest advocates of Canada that she has ever had, not from any superficial knowledge of the country, but because of a very intimate knowledge obtained by meeting the people in every part of this great Dominion. He does not meet them in state, but on these trips he meets them in heart to heart talk and in hand in hand conversation. He knows the aspirations of the Canadian people in the lower as well as in the higher walks of life, If they continue to send men to us like the present Governor General, Canada may be proud and more than satisfied at the present mode of selection.

Since the Minister of Railways has just made reference to the advisability of consulting the various classes in Canada, I should like to suggest that there are at least some classes in this country who are not highly satisfied with maintaining an office of this kind. I have no word of criticism whatever with regard to the present occupant of that office; I am speaking solely of the office itself, of the effect it has in this country, and of the expenditure that is involved. Although it may help to unite us to Great Britain, and I am not suggesting that we should sever in any way that union, there is not the slightest doubt that it does tend to perpetuate certain class distinctions in this country that are foreign to the essential democracy which had; existed here in the earlier years, and which some of us would like to see perpetuated. It is all very well to talk about the Governor General knowing all classes of people, but to no small extent a miniature court is maintained! here for the sake of a comparatively small group of people in the city of Ottawa and others who may be able to travel here on special occasions. I think that is being felt throughout Canada by a large number of those people across the country who the Minister of Railways said it is well should be consulted in matters of this kind.
Further than that, in a large number of our papers within the last year or two there have been estimates made as to the expenditure involved in the upkeep of this particular office. It is very difficult to know just what these expenditures are, because they are scattered among so many items in different parts of the estimates. I should say the expenditure is somewhere near $300,000, which is very directly required in connection with the upkeep of this office. In addition to that, we should include interest on the money in-275
vested in Rideau Hall, and we then have an expenditure of about $500,000 a year for this one official. Now one might imagine that this little country of Canada, large in geographical area, but very small in population, and very small in resources, ought at this time to pay some little attention to these huge amounts that are being thrown around on every hand. I urge, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come when we should begin to economize along those lines that are at least essential to the real welfare of the great masses of the people.
Further, may I say a few words with regard to the selection of a new Governor General. None of us like to speak about the matter when the new Governor General has actually been appointed, but now, when no one is apparently in sight, so far as we are informed, why not consider the type of person to be appointed to that office? I would join with one or two others who have spoken in suggesting that we might very well abolish that office here in Canada. I cannot see why the Chief Justice might not fulfil the formal functions that are now filled by the Governor General. If we must have a Governor General in Canada, why should he not be a Canadian? It seems to me that if we are so reduced by our party squabbles in this country that we cannot manage to unite in selecting some outstanding Canadian who would fitly occupy a position of that kind, then the future of this country is dark indeed. Surely there are individuals in Canada who could adequately fill an office of this kind. I cannot see why if we pride ourselves, as we sometimes do, on being one of the independent members of the commonwealth of British people, we should1 continue to occupy a position which is essentially one of subserviency to the Mother Country.
Then again, if we are to have a representative from the Old Country, I do not know why we ought always select someone from the nobility, or from the nearest approach to the nobility that we can find. We have had within the past year or so the rise of a new democracy in the Old Land. We have seen for a short time occupying office in the Old Country the Labour party. I do not know whether they are coming back to office in the near future; I think they will at no distant future. But in any case why should we not have a representative of what might be termed the common people, rather than have sent over to us one who represents the aristocracy? We have claimed in this country to belong to the common people. We consist very largely -of ordinary business people, far-

mere and labouring people. Why should we have sent to us individuals who belong to another type, who are the survivors of the feudalism of the Old Land, which we have tried to get rid of on this North American continent? I should like to suggest that when the government is making any suggestions, or however this matter is arranged, these considerations might very well be kept in mind, and thus we might try to bring our institutions a little more into harmony with the ideals that are generally prevalent throughout Canada.
